newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada oil lobby seeks to stop proposed MMT ban.
newsitem.headline: Canada oil lobby seeks to stop proposed MMT ban.

text.p: The Canadian Petroleum Products Institute (CPPI), the main oil industry lobby group, on Tuesday urged the Canadian government to drop a bill banning the gasoline additive MMT.
The proposed legislation, which would ban the sale and imports of the widely used octane-enhancer, has reached a final debate stage in Canada's parliament and faces an imminent House of Commons vote.
The institute on Tuesday released a study, disputing previous auto industry research which had concluded that MMT gums up auto emission diagnostic systems.
"We believe to some extent that perhaps the government has been mislead on this issue," said CPPI vice-president Brendan Hawley.
CPPI has repeatedly asked the govenment to conduct an independent evaluation before banning MMT.
But Environment Ministry spokesman Roger White said that the government would press the bill forward, regardless of all efforts to stop it.
"The government is convinced that the bill is the right approach," White said.

Last month, Richmond, Va.-based Ethyl Corp threatened Ottawa with a US$201 million lawsuit under the North American Free Trade Agreement over the proposed MMT legislation. Ethyl's Canadian subsidiary, Ethyl Canada, is the only importer and manufacturer of MMT in the country.
Environment and health groups claim that MMT, because of its key ingredient, manganese, is a potential neuro-toxin that might hurt brain development.
MMT, methylcyclopentadienyl manganese tricarbonyl, has been used as a replacement for lead in gasoline in Canada since 1977.
The use of the controversial additive was allowed in the United States in late 1995 after a U.S. Court of Appeals overruled Environmental Protection Agency objections to it.
